bib.title: Chapter 4. Regression and Prediction (Practical Statistics for Data Scientists)
bib.venue: book chapter (O'Reilly); copyright line: 2017 Datastats, LLC

question: How are regression models fit, assessed, interpreted and diagnosed, and how should a data scientist use them for prediction?
contributions: Teaches simple and multiple linear regression, model selection, prediction/confidence intervals, factor variables, interpretation pitfalls, diagnostics and nonlinear terms, all on King County housing data in R.

limits: Equations are stripped from the cached text, so formulas (OLS solution, RMSE, RSE, R2, hat-value and Cook's distance thresholds) are not recorded.
Single running dataset (King County house sales); R code only, no Python.
Sample size is given only through the degrees of freedom (22683 df, 5 predictors); no dataset size or date range is stated.
Chapter says p-values, F and R2 are in-sample; it does not cover GLMs, logistic regression or regularisation beyond naming ridge and lasso.
practices: Use RMSE as the main metric for comparing regression models in data science (Assessing the Model).
Treat R2, F and p-values as in-sample metrics; validate with a holdout or k-fold cross-validation (Cross-Validation).
Prefer simpler models; use AIC (2P + n log(RSS/n)) with stepwise search rather than RMSE or R2, which always improve with more variables (Model Selection).
Cross-validate stepwise and subset selection since they are in-sample and can overfit.
Do not extrapolate beyond the range of the fit data (Dangers of Extrapolation).
Use a prediction interval, not a confidence interval, for individual predictions; a confidence interval greatly underestimates the uncertainty (Prediction Interval or Confidence Interval).
Code a factor with P levels as P-1 dummies in regression to avoid multicollinearity; keep one-hot for trees and nearest neighbours (Dummy Variables).
Consolidate many-level factors, ideally by grouping on residuals from an initial model (Factor Variables with Many Levels).
Remove variables until multicollinearity is gone (Multicollinearity).
Check for omitted confounders before reading coefficients causally; regression does not prove causation (Confounding Variables; Prediction versus Explanation).
Add interaction terms when a predictor's effect depends on another, found by domain knowledge, stepwise, penalized regression or tree models (Interactions and Main Effects).
Inspect standardized residuals for outliers and use them for anomaly detection; in big data outliers rarely matter for the fit (Outliers).
Use partial residual plots to detect nonlinearity, the most important diagnostic after outlier detection (Partial Residual Plots).
Prefer splines or GAMs over high-order polynomials, which become wiggly; spline coefficients are read from plots, not directly (Splines).
Residual distribution matters little for prediction; heteroskedasticity can signal a missing predictor (Heteroskedasticity).

terms.definition: The difference between the observed values and the fitted values.
The method of fitting a regression by minimizing the sum of squared residuals.
The square root of the average squared error of the regression (this is the most widely used metric to compare regression models).
The same as the root mean squared error, but adjusted for degrees of freedom.
The proportion of variance explained by the model, from 0 to 1.
The coefficient for a predictor, divided by the standard error of the coefficient, giving a metric to compare the importance of variables in the model.
An uncertainty interval around an individual predicted value.
Extension of a model beyond the range of the data used to fit it.
The most common type of coding used by statisticians, in which one level of a factor is used as a reference and other factors are compared to that level.
A common type of coding used in the machine learning community in which all factors levels are retained.
When the predictor variables have perfect, or near-perfect, correlation, the regression can be unstable or impossible to compute.

code.snippet:
house_lm <- lm(AdjSalePrice ~ SqFtTotLiving + SqFtLot + Bathrooms +
                 Bedrooms + BldgGrade,
               data=house, na.action=na.omit)

knots <- quantile(house_98105$SqFtTotLiving, p=c(.25, .5, .75))
lm_spline <- lm(AdjSalePrice ~ bs(SqFtTotLiving, knots=knots, degree=3) +
  SqFtLot + Bathrooms + Bedrooms + BldgGrade,  data=house_98105)
